kappaBand: Kappa interpretation (Landis and Koch, 1977): below 0.20 slight, 0.21-0.40 fair, 0.41-0.60 moderate, 0.61-0.80 substantial, 0.81 and above almost perfect.
mhNote: Miles and Huberman (1994) agreement = units coded by both / (coded by both + coded by only one). The authors suggest about 80% at first and about 90% eventually.
alphaNote: Krippendorff (2004): 0.80 and above is considered reliable; 0.667-0.80 is acceptable for tentative conclusions only.

helpBody.genel:
A browser tool for coding text data such as interview transcripts, open-ended survey answers and documents. Nothing to install, no internet connection used, and your data stays on your computer.

  1. Add your documents from the left panel.
  2. Select a passage and give it a code.
  3. Collect every instance of a code in Quotations.
  4. Explore frequencies, matrices and the code map in Analysis.
  5. With two coders, calculate agreement.
  6. Download a Word report from Report.

Click the ? next to any section to see what it is for.

ipucu.belgeler: The texts you will analyse: interview transcripts, open-ended answers, documents. Add .txt, .md, .docx or .pdf files or paste the text. The number shows how many codings the document has. Double-click to rename.
ipucu.kodlar: The labels you give to the text. Drag a code onto another to make it a subcode, so codes are grouped under themes. Click a code to outline where it occurs in the text.
ipucu.okuyucu:
Select a passage with the mouse and type a code name in the box that opens, or pick one from the list.

The coloured stripes on the left show where each coding starts and ends. Click a coded passage to add a memo, change the code or remove it in the right panel.
ipucu.ozellikler: Participant details such as gender, age or year. You can filter quotations by them, for example to see only what female participants said. For many participants, import them from a table in the Tools menu.
ipucu.belgeNot: Your notes about this document: date, length and setting of the interview, first impressions.
ipucu.kodlayici: Used to tell who made each coding. In a reliability study two people code under different names.
ipucu.kor: When on, you only see your own codings. This keeps the second coder from being influenced by the first.
ipucu.geriAl: Undoes the last action (Ctrl+Z) or redoes what was undone (Ctrl+Y).
ipucu.fAra: Searches the text and memos of the quotations.
ipucu.fOzellik: Shows only quotations from documents with the selected attribute, for example "Gender: Female".
ipucu.fKodlar: Choose which codes' quotations you want to see. With "Include subcodes" ticked, selecting a theme selects all codes under it.
ipucu.alintiListe: Every passage coded with the selected codes, ready to use as direct quotations in your findings. "Show in document" takes you back to its context.
ipucu.istat: Overview of the project. "Text coded" is the share of all text marked with at least one code.
ipucu.frekans: How many times and in how many documents each code was used. Statements such as "more than half of the participants..." come from this table.
ipucu.kelime: The most frequent words, ignoring function words. Useful for ideas before you start coding.
ipucu.matris: Rows are codes and columns are documents. Each cell shows how many times the code was used in that document, so you can see which theme stands out for which participant.
ipucu.esgorunum: How often two codes overlap on the same passage. Codes that often co-occur may belong to the same theme.
ipucu.harita: A diagram of your theme structure. Circle size shows how often a code is used and the arcs on the right show codes that co-occur. Download it as SVG to use as a figure.
ipucu.uyumBirim: How the text is split for comparison. Paragraphs are more lenient, sentences are stricter. Only documents coded by both coders are included.
ipucu.colBoth: Units where both coders applied this code.
ipucu.colOnlyA: Units where only the first coder applied this code.
ipucu.colOnlyB: Units where only the second coder applied this code.
ipucu.colNeither: Units where neither coder applied this code.
ipucu.colAgree: Simple percent agreement: the share of units where both made the same decision. It tends to be high because uncoded units also count.
ipucu.colMH: Miles and Huberman agreement: looks only at units coded by at least one coder.
ipucu.colKappa: Cohen's kappa: corrects for agreement by chance. Preferred by international journals.
ipucu.alfa: Krippendorff's alpha: for two or more coders and tolerant of missing data. 0.80 and above is considered reliable.
ipucu.ayrisma: Passages where the two coders differ. Reading them together and sharpening the code definitions improves reliability.
ipucu.birlestir: Adds a project file in which a colleague coded the same documents. Documents are matched by their text.
ipucu.rWord: The codebook, frequency table, matrix, quotations, agreement table and project log in one Word file.
ipucu.rCsv: A table with one row per coding. Opens in Excel, SPSS or R.
ipucu.rKitapCsv: Code names, definitions, parents and usage counts.
ipucu.rProje: The whole project (documents, codes, codings, memos). Use it for backups or to move to another computer.
ipucu.qdpx: REFI-QDA is the common file format of qualitative analysis programs. Open your project in NVivo, MAXQDA or ATLAS.ti, or open their projects here.
ipucu.kodTanim: A short definition of when to use the code. It appears in the codebook and guides the second coder.
ipucu.kodNot: Your analytic notes about this code: why you created it, how it relates to others, how it changed.
ipucu.ikinciDosya: Prepares a file with the documents and codebook but no codings, with blind coding on. When your colleague sends it back coded, merge it with "Add another coder's file".
ipucu.anonim: Replaces real names with pseudonyms. Use it before sharing transcripts, for ethics approval and data protection.
ipucu.araKodla: Finds every place a word occurs and applies the chosen code in one go. You can review the results one by one before applying.

giris.baslik: Code your interviews, find the themes, get your report.
giris.alt: Coding Desk is a free tool that helps you analyse qualitative text data (interview transcripts, focus group records, open-ended survey answers, documents) in an orderly and evidence-based way. Nothing to install, no internet connection; your data never leaves your computer.
giris.ornekNot: To get to know the tool, start with the sample project: three invented student interviews, already coded.
giris.ne1: Say you interviewed 20 students about distance learning and ended up with 40 pages of transcripts. Marking them with a highlighter on paper and collecting quotations by hand takes days. Answering reviewers' questions (how many participants said this, who did the coding, how reliable is it) is hard to back up with evidence.
giris.ne2: Coding Desk does this on the computer. You select a sentence and give it a code; the tool gathers every instance of each code, counts how many participants mention each theme, calculates how far two coders agree, and turns the results into a Word report you can use in your thesis or article.
adimlar: Upload Word, PDF or text files, or paste the text. Import participant details from an Excel table.
Select a sentence you find important and give it a name. Group similar codes under themes.
Click a code to list everything said about it, with who said it, on one page.
See patterns with code frequencies, a matrix by participant, co-occurring codes and a code map.
A colleague codes the same documents separately; the tool calculates agreement with Miles-Huberman, kappa and alpha.
Codebook, tables, quotations and agreement results in a Word file with one click.
kimler: Master's and doctoral students writing qualitative or mixed-methods theses
Academics doing interview, focus group or document analysis
Researchers and institutions analysing open-ended survey answers
Lecturers and students in qualitative research methods courses
guven: This work is usually done with programs that charge a yearly licence fee. Coding Desk is free and open source (MIT licence).
The tool is a single file that runs in your browser. Interview data is never sent to a server, which matters for data protection and ethics approval.
The common file format of NVivo, MAXQDA and ATLAS.ti (REFI-QDA) is supported, so you can move your work to or from these programs.
ozGruplar: Code by selecting text, subcodes and themes
Quotations by code, participant and coder
Blind coding and a file for a second coder
Word report, CSV and project log
File exchange with NVivo, MAXQDA, ATLAS.ti

aciklama.giris: A total of {0} comparisons were made (each code for each unit). In {1} of them you both applied the code, in {2} only {5} did, in {3} only {6} did, and in {4} neither of you did.
aciklama.basitNe: The share of comparisons where both coders made the same decision.
aciklama.basitUyari: It tends to be high because places where the code was not applied also count as agreement; do not report it on its own.
aciklama.mhNe: Looks only at places where at least one of you applied the code and ignores places you both left blank, so it is stricter than simple agreement.
aciklama.mhEsik: Miles and Huberman (1994) suggest about 80% at first and about 90% as the analysis matures.
mhSonuc: low; review the code definitions together
aciklama.kappaNe: Two people coding at random would still agree sometimes. Kappa shows how far the real agreement is above this chance agreement. 0 is chance level, 1 is perfect agreement.
aciklama.kappaHesap: Observed agreement {0}, agreement expected by chance {1}; kappa = ({0} - {1}) / (1 - {1}) = {2}
aciklama.alfaNe: Same idea as kappa, but it also works with more than two coders and with coders who did not code every document.
aciklama.alfaHesap: All coders and codes together: alpha = {0}
aciklama.hangisi: Which should I report? International journals usually expect kappa or alpha; Miles-Huberman agreement is also common. The safest choice is to report Miles-Huberman together with kappa. The Report tab contains a method paragraph prepared with these numbers.

atif.baslik: How do I cite this tool?
atif.ne: If you used Coding Desk, please cite it in your method section. This supports its development and keeps it free.
